content: Suppose a candle and a converging lens are fixed while a screen slides behind the lens. How can I predict where the sharp image will appear, and what changes as the candle moves farther from the focal point?

Use the thin-lens relation, 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i, with a consistent sign convention. For an object outside the focal length, the calculated positive image distance locates a sharp real image behind the lens. Moving the candle farther away brings the image closer to the focal plane. Its size also decreases, since the magnitude of the lateral magnification is d_i/d_o.
Why does the image orientation change at all? Rays from the candle top can pass through many parts of the lens, so it is not obvious why they should consistently arrive below the optical axis.

All those rays begin at the same upper object point, but the lens redirects them so they converge at one corresponding image point below the axis. A ray through the optical center is especially useful for seeing the geometry because, in the thin-lens approximation, it continues nearly straight. The converging bundle crosses the axis before reaching the screen, mapping the object's top below its bottom.

I might be wrong, but I think a converging lens forms an inverted real image on the opposite side when the object lies beyond its focal point...? If so, is the ray crossing what makes both “real” and “inverted” true?

That description is right for an ideal converging lens with the object beyond one focal length. “Real” means the refracted rays physically converge on the opposite side, so a screen can intercept the image. “Inverted” describes the mapping: rays from points above and below the axis converge below and above it, respectively. The crossing geometry connects the two features, although the terms describe different properties.
What special result occurs when the candle is exactly twice the focal length from the lens? I would like to compare the image position and size there with cases just inside and outside that distance.

At d_o = 2f, the equation gives d_i = 2f, so the image forms twice the focal length away on the opposite side. Its magnification is -1: equal in size and inverted. If the candle moves between f and 2f, the image moves beyond 2f and grows. If the candle moves beyond 2f, the image lies between f and 2f and shrinks.
If an arrow is projected through a converging lens onto a wall, which observations distinguish a real image from a virtual one without relying only on whether the picture looks sharp to an eye?

A real image can be brought into focus directly on the wall because light from each object point physically converges at a corresponding point there. A virtual image cannot be caught on a bare wall at its apparent location; it is seen by looking into the outgoing rays. Moving the wall through the predicted image plane and finding a focused projection is therefore the clearest test.

Does the side of the lens settle the question by itself? A projected image appears behind the lens relative to the arrow, but an observer can stand in several places and still describe directions differently.

It is better to name the incident side and outgoing side rather than use viewpoint-dependent words like behind. For a single converging lens with a real object, a real image forms on the outgoing side because that is where refracted rays can meet. Side is a useful clue, but physical convergence is the defining test, and more complicated multi-lens systems require especially careful labeling.

I might be wrong, but I think a converging lens forms an upright real image on the opposite side when the object lies beyond its focal point...? Would that follow because every object point is reproduced directly across from itself?

The real image is on the opposite side, but for this single-lens arrangement it is inverted, not upright. Corresponding points are not transferred straight across at the same height: a point above the axis sends a bundle that converges below it, while a lower point maps above. An upright real image is possible in a larger optical system, but it requires additional imaging stages or reflections.
Could the same arrow ever look upright through this one lens while remaining impossible to project on the wall? Where must the arrow be placed, and what would moving the wall reveal?

Yes. Place the arrow closer to the converging lens than its focal length and look through the lens from the outgoing side. You see an upright, magnified virtual image that appears on the arrow's side. Sliding a wall around that apparent position will never produce a sharp image, because no rays actually meet there; only their backward extensions do.
Why can a magnifying glass enlarge print without forming a bright copy on the table? The letters seem to occupy a definite place, yet moving a sheet there does not capture them.

With the print inside the focal length, the lens makes the outgoing rays less divergent but does not bring them together. Your eye receives those rays and traces their directions backward to an apparent, enlarged source. That apparent source is the virtual image. A sheet cannot capture it because no focused light pattern exists at that location, whereas your eye adds its own focusing step to form a real retinal image.

How does bringing the print toward the focal point affect the apparent image? I can see that its angular size changes, but the connection between image distance, linear magnification, and viewing position is unclear.

As the print approaches the focal point from inside, the virtual image moves farther away and the magnitude of its linear magnification grows. At the focal point, the outgoing rays are parallel and the virtual image is effectively at infinity. What your eye perceives is angular magnification, which also depends on eye position and accommodation, so it is related to—but not identical with—the lens's linear magnification.

I might be wrong, but I think an object inside a converging lens's focal length produces an upright, magnified virtual image on the object's side...? Is backward ray tracing the reason for assigning that side?

Yes. The refracted rays leave the lens diverging, and extending them backward makes them intersect on the object's side. That intersection defines the virtual image position. It is upright because the apparent top remains above the axis, and it is magnified because the backward extensions meet farther from the lens than the object does. The construction locates an apparent source; it does not imply light travels backward.
If another converging lens is added after the magnifier, can it convert that virtual image into something a screen records? How should the first image be treated when analyzing the second lens?

It can, provided the second lens redirects the actual outgoing bundle so those rays converge. For the second lens, use the vergence of the arriving rays to identify its effective object location and apply a consistent sign convention. The first lens's virtual image can serve as an object for the second stage, but the second lens acts on real rays, not on the backward extensions themselves.
A lens diagram often draws a virtual image using dashed lines. What exactly do those dashed segments represent, and how can they locate an image when no light follows them through space?

The solid segments show the actual paths of light after refraction. The dashed segments extend those paths backward in straight lines to identify where the diverging bundle appears to originate. Their intersection gives the virtual image location. This is physically meaningful because the outgoing wavefront has the same local directions as light spreading from that apparent point, even though no ray travels along the dashed paths.

When the object moves from just outside the focal point to just inside it, what changes continuously and what changes category? I am especially curious about the image passing through an infinite distance.

Approaching the focal point from outside, the real image recedes toward infinity and its magnitude grows. At the focal point, ideal outgoing rays are parallel. Moving just inside makes them slightly divergent, so their backward extensions meet at a distant virtual image on the incident side. Vergence changes continuously through zero, while the labels switch from real and inverted to virtual and upright.

I might be wrong, but I think an object inside a converging lens's focal length produces an upright, magnified virtual image on the lens's opposite side...? Could the dashed intersection be interpreted there instead?

The upright, magnified, virtual parts fit, but the side does not. After the lens, the actual rays diverge on the outgoing side; extending them backward makes the dashed lines meet on the object's side. Extending them farther forward cannot create a common intersection. The opposite side contains the diverging real rays, while the virtual image is their apparent origin on the incident side.
How would a sign convention encode that distinction in the thin-lens equation? Please relate the sign of image distance to the physical ray behavior rather than giving only a memorized rule.

In the common real-is-positive convention, d_o is positive for the real object and d_i is negative for this virtual image. Substituting d_o < f into 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i forces that negative result. Geometrically, positive d_i denotes an actual convergence on the outgoing side; negative d_i denotes an apparent source found by backward extension on the incident side.
When a broad beam of parallel light enters a converging lens, does every ray head toward the same location, or does the answer depend on the beam's angle relative to the optical axis?

Direction matters. In ideal paraxial optics, rays parallel to the optical axis converge at the rear focal point. A collimated beam tilted slightly to the axis converges at a displaced point in the rear focal plane. Thus a distant scene maps different incoming directions to different positions across that plane, which is the basic focusing action used by cameras and telescopes.
Why is it called a focal plane rather than simply a focus? If the incoming bundle has one direction, it still seems that only one point should matter for that bundle.

For one chosen direction, one focal point does matter. The word “plane” collects the focal points associated with many nearby incoming directions. An on-axis bundle lands at the axial focus; tilted bundles land at other transverse positions. Under the ideal thin-lens and paraxial approximations, those points lie on a plane one focal length from the lens, though real systems may have field curvature.

I might be wrong, but I think parallel rays entering an ideal converging thin lens meet at its focal plane after refraction through the lens...? Does “parallel” include bundles tilted away from the axis?

That is the ideal thin-lens picture, with one useful refinement: each parallel bundle meets at a point in the focal plane, and the point depends on the bundle's direction. Axial parallel rays meet at the axial focal point; a tilted collimated bundle meets off axis. The statement assumes paraxial rays, so very large field angles or aperture angles require a more complete aberration-aware model.
If the lens aperture is widened while the incoming beam remains collimated, why can the spot stop shrinking? I want to separate diffraction from spherical aberration in that limiting case.

A wider aperture reduces the diffraction-limited Airy disk because it admits a larger wavefront. However, a spherical lens bends marginal rays differently from paraxial rays, so their geometric intersections spread along the axis and enlarge the spot near the chosen plane. At small apertures diffraction dominates; at large apertures spherical aberration may dominate. The sharpest result often occurs at an intermediate aperture.

White light passing through a converging lens can produce colored edges near focus. Is that mainly because colors travel at different speeds in glass, or because the lens sends them along different paths?

The imaging error comes from different paths and focal powers. The refractive index of glass varies with wavelength, so the surfaces deflect wavelengths by different amounts. In many ordinary glasses, blue light is bent more strongly than red and comes to an axial focus closer to a positive lens. Their differing speeds inside glass underlie dispersion, but the visible blur follows from the resulting spatial separation.
Would a narrow laser beam avoid that separation even if it crosses the lens far from the center? I am wondering whether using one wavelength removes every reason for a spread of focal positions.

A nearly monochromatic laser removes chromatic focal separation, since it supplies essentially one wavelength. It does not remove geometric aberrations. A ray bundle crossing far from the center can still suffer spherical aberration, coma, or astigmatism, depending on aperture and field angle. Diffraction and imperfections also give the focus finite size, so monochromatic light does not guarantee a single infinitesimal spot.

I might be wrong, but I think parallel rays entering any real converging lens meet at one identical focal point regardless of their wavelength...? Would dispersion merely change their travel time without changing that location?

Dispersion generally changes the location as well as the travel time. Because refractive index depends on wavelength, a real converging lens usually has a different focal length for each color; even same-direction parallel bundles need not share one focus. Aberrations can also keep rays of a single wavelength from meeting identically. Achromatic designs combine glasses and powers to bring selected wavelengths close to a common focus, but not every wavelength perfectly.
How does an achromatic doublet choose which colors to align, and what residual error remains between or beyond those wavelengths? Does refocusing the sensor remove the remaining colored fringe?

Designers typically balance a positive low-dispersion element with a negative higher-dispersion element so two selected wavelengths have the same focal power while the pair remains converging. Other wavelengths follow slightly different dispersion curves, leaving secondary spectrum. Refocusing can favor another wavelength or minimize a weighted blur, but it cannot make all separated focal surfaces coincide. More elaborate apochromatic systems reduce the residual further.

A thick lens has two curved surfaces separated by glass, yet elementary diagrams replace it with one line. From which location should object and image distances actually be measured when the thickness is not negligible?

Use the lens's principal planes. A thick optical element generally has a front principal plane for the object-side conjugate and a rear principal plane for the image-side conjugate. These planes summarize the first-order effect of propagation and refraction through both surfaces. They need not coincide with either surface, lie at the lens center, or even remain inside the glass.

How can an imaginary reference plane determine a measurable focus? It sounds like a bookkeeping device, so I am trying to understand which ray properties remain unchanged when the real lens is replaced.

It is a bookkeeping device with measurable consequences. In first-order optics, the principal planes let you replace a thick system by an equivalent refraction of the same optical power while preserving object-image conjugacy and transverse magnification. Rays still enter and leave at the real surfaces; the equivalent construction relocates where distances and ray heights are referenced so the simple Gaussian relations reproduce the system's external behavior.

I might be wrong, but I think the thin-lens equation relates focal length to object and image distances measured from the lens's principal plane...? For a thick lens, should that become two separate principal planes?

Yes, with that distinction. An ideal thin lens has coincident principal planes, represented by the single lens plane, so both distances are referenced there. For a thick lens or compound system, measure object distance from the front principal plane and image distance from the rear principal plane. Using those conjugate distances preserves the familiar equation, provided focal length and signs follow the same cardinal-point convention.
If one principal plane lies outside the glass, is a negative physical distance to the nearest surface a problem? How would an experiment locate the effective plane without opening the lens?

There is no problem; cardinal points are effective locations and need not occupy material. One practical method measures the system's effective focal length and its front and back focal distances. The offsets between the focal points and the respective principal planes then follow from those quantities. Optical benches can obtain them by collimated illumination, nodal-slide methods, or conjugate measurements, all without accessing the lens interior.

Which reference point on a converging lens makes the object-distance measurement unambiguous? Choosing the front vertex, center of the glass, or aperture seems capable of changing the numerical prediction for a nearby object.

For the Gaussian imaging equation, the proper reference is a principal plane, not the aperture or an arbitrarily chosen glass point. In the ideal thin-lens model, the two principal planes coincide at the drawn lens plane, making the choice look like the center. For a real thick lens, the front and rear principal planes are distinct, and the surface vertices serve only as convenient mechanical references.
Does measuring from a surface become harmless when the lens is symmetric? Both curvatures then mirror each other, but the glass still has thickness and the ray travels between refractions.

Symmetry can place the principal planes symmetrically within the element, but it does not generally put them on the surfaces. Measuring from a vertex therefore introduces an offset. The approximation may be harmless when thickness is tiny relative to the relevant distances and required accuracy, yet it becomes important for short focal lengths, close conjugates, or multi-element systems where principal planes can shift substantially.

I might be wrong, but I think the thin-lens equation relates focal length to object and image distances measured from the lens's nearest surface...? Would using whichever surface faces each conjugate account for the thickness?

Using the nearest surfaces does not, by itself, account for thickness. The standard thin-lens equation assumes distances measured from the coincident principal plane of the idealized lens. For a thick lens, use the front principal plane for object distance and the rear principal plane for image distance. Surface-based distances can still be used, but only after adding the appropriate principal-plane offsets or applying a thick-lens matrix model.
What kind of prediction error results if those offsets are ignored: a constant shift in focus, a change in magnification, or both? I am considering objects at several different distances.

Both can be wrong. Referencing the conjugates to surfaces changes the distances inserted into a nonlinear reciprocal relation, so the resulting focus error is not generally one constant correction across object positions. The computed magnification, which depends on the conjugate-distance ratio, also changes. Far from the lens the discrepancy may look nearly like a fixed back-focus offset, while close-object calculations expose stronger distance-dependent errors.
